Units and the dictionary

Source: vignettes/units.Rmd
units.Rmd

This article is for authors whose numbers have units, and for projects that fix some values by choice: a trigger level, a reporting year, the name of a study area. After it you will be able to print a number with its unit in the right form, convert it as you print it, give weft the names of your own units, and keep a project’s chosen values in one dictionary file that every document and pipeline reads.

library(weft)

Quantities

A quantity is a number with a unit. u() makes one. The unit is written as it is, never evaluated as R, or as a string:

u(35, m)
#> 35 [m]
u(5, mg/L)
#> 5 [mg/L]
u(150, "CFU/100 mL")
#> 150 [CFU/(100mL)]

u() is a short form of units::set_units(), and all arithmetic is the units package’s. Units combine, cancel and convert, and adding two units that do not convert is an error:

u(3, m) + u(20, cm)
#> 3.2 [m]
u(3, m) / u(50, cm)
#> 6 [1]
u(3, m) + u(2, kg)
#> Error:
#> ! cannot convert kg into m

A quantity cannot be compared with a bare number. A check states its unit:

claim(u(3, m), . > 2)
#> Error:
#> ! weft: 1 failed claim
#>   check `. > 2` raised an error: both operands of the expression should be "units" objects (value: 3 [m])
#>     state the check's unit, as in . < u(0.45, ug) (rule 4.4.5)
claim(u(3, m), . > u(2, m))
#> 3 [m]

Printing a quantity

A formatter prints the unit after the number, separated by a no-break space. You do not type the unit in the prose.

fmt_num(u(35, m))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "35 m"
fmt_num(u(1.2, m^2))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "1.2 m^2^"
fmt_num(u(20, degC))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "20 °C"
fmt_num(u(35, "%"))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "35%"
fmt_num(u(7.2, pH))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "pH 7.2"

The symbol text is Pandoc markdown, so m^2^ renders as a superscript. Some units have no space before them (%, °), and pH goes before the number.

Symbol or name

A unit prints in one of two forms: its symbol (“5 m”) or its name (“five metres”). By default the form follows the number: digits take the symbol, and a spelled number takes the name.

fmt_num(u(3, m))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "3 m"
fmt_word(u(3, m))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "three metres"

Three unit classes choose the form for one value: .usym the symbol, .uname the name, .nounit no unit at all. In R code the same choice is the unit_form argument:

fmt_num(u(5, m), unit_form = "name")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "5 metres"
fmt_num(u(1, m), unit_form = "name")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "1 metre"
fmt_num(u(5, m), unit_form = "none")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "5"
fmt_num(u(12, NTU), unit_form = "name")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "12 nephelometric turbidity units"

A name is singular only when its number prints as “1” or “one”. The setting unit_form (auto, symbol or name) in _weft.yml, or under a document’s weft: key, changes the default for a project or a document.

fmt_unit() prints the unit alone, for a table heading:

fmt_unit(u(5, mg/L))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "mg/L"
fmt_unit(u(5, mg/L), unit_form = "name")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "milligrams per litre"

Converting as you print

The key unit="m" on a value or a span, and the argument unit in R code, print the quantity in another unit. The number, the unit and the arm a span chooses are all in that unit:

fmt_num(u(150, cm), unit = "m")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "1.5 m"

A ladder is a list of units you accept, separated by |. weft prints the quantity in the first unit that gives a number from 1 up to 1,000:

fmt_num(u(2500, m), unit = "mm|m|km")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "2.5 km"
fmt_num(u(0.004, m), unit = "mm|m|km")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "4 mm"

A vector takes one unit for all its numbers, the one where most of them fit:

fmt_num(u(c(0.4, 2500), m), unit = "mm|m|km")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "400 mm"       "2,500,000 mm"

Inside a pipe-table cell, write the ladder’s bars as \|.

Lists of quantities

A list prints the unit once, after the last item. .pairs, .ul, .ol and .dl print it with each item.

fmt_and(fmt_num(u(c(3, 5, 7), m)))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "3, 5 and 7 m"
fmt_range(u(c(3, 5), m))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "3–5 m"

Quantities that print as zero

A small quantity that prints as “0.0” records the same warned check as a plain number, and the message suggests a prefixed unit where one would help:

fmt_num(u(0.04, m))
#> Warning: weft: 0.04 printed as 0.0: add sigfig to show it, or digits to confirm
#> it; or show it in a prefixed unit, such as unit = "mm"
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "0.0 m"

In a document

This document reads a project dictionary and a units: table, both shown further down.

---
title: "Units"
output: html_document
knitr:
  opts_knit:
    weft: !expr weft::weft_setup()
weft:
  dict_local:
    lab_sites:
      value: 4
      type: number
      definition: "Sites sent to the laboratory in this chapter."
      why: "Only the autumn survey sent samples away."
---

```{r data}
depth <- u(c(0.42, 0.65, 1.31), m)
visited <- u(12, sites)
core <- u(150, cm)
last_year <- 2024
```

The reach is `r dict$reach_len`{.num} long, or `r dict$reach_len`{unit="m"}.

Depths were `r depth`{.num .and}, a range of `r range(depth)`{.range}.

We visited `r visited`{.num}, and the cores were `r core`{.uname unit="m"} long.

[# core was | # cores were]{n="core" unit="m"} kept.

Turbidity above `r dict$trigger`{.num} is reported.

Salinity is logged to `r dict$salinity_res`{.uname}, or `r dict$salinity_res`{.uname sigfig="1"}.

Records start in `r dict$first_year`, and the logger ran for `r last_year - dict$first_year`{.word} years.

`r dict_local$lab_sites`{.word .cap} sites went to the laboratory.

The first depth was `r depth[1]`.

It renders as:

The reach is 2 km long, or 2,000 m.

Depths were 0.4, 0.7 and 1.3 m, a range of 0.4–1.3 m.

We visited 12 sites, and the cores were 1.5 metres long.

1.5 m cores were kept.

Turbidity above 10 NTU is reported.

Salinity is logged to 0.0 practical salinity units, or 0.01 practical
salinity units.

Records start in 2014, and the logger ran for ten years.

Four sites went to the laboratory.

The first depth was 0.42.

and the knit ends with two warnings, which do not fail the render:

weft: 2 warned check(s)
  units.Rmd:33  [printed as zero] `r dict$salinity_res`
      0.01 printed as 0.0: add sigfig to show it, or digits to confirm it
  units.Rmd:39  [unit warning] `r depth[1]`
      weft: `r depth[1]` is a quantity (0.42) and its unit is not printed. Add `{.num}` to print it with its unit, or `{.nounit}` to say the unit is not wanted (rule 4.4.10).

A bare value prints a quantity as knitr prints it, without the unit, and weft warns because the reader loses the unit. Add {.num} to print it, or {.nounit} to say you meant to drop it.

Units weft does not know

weft starts from the units package’s database, and adds a table of its own for units common in environmental reports:

unit_defaults()[, c("unit", "is", "name", "symbol", "before")]
#>          unit       is                         name     symbol before
#> 1          pH     base                           pH       <NA>   TRUE
#> 2         mph   1 mi/h                mile per hour       <NA>  FALSE
#> 3         nmi   1852 m                nautical mile       <NA>  FALSE
#> 4          Ma    1 Myr                million years       <NA>  FALSE
#> 5          ka    1 kyr               thousand years       <NA>  FALSE
#> 6         gal 1 gallon                       gallon       <NA>  FALSE
#> 7         ppm     <NA>             part per million       <NA>  FALSE
#> 8         ppb     <NA>             part per billion       <NA>  FALSE
#> 9         NTU     base nephelometric turbidity unit       <NA>  FALSE
#> 10        PSU     base      practical salinity unit       <NA>  FALSE
#> 11        CFU     base          colony-forming unit       <NA>  FALSE
#> 12        MPN     base                         <NA>       <NA>  FALSE
#> 13 CFU/100 mL     <NA>                         <NA> CFU/100 mL  FALSE
#> 14 MPN/100 mL     <NA>                         <NA> MPN/100 mL  FALSE

A unit that neither knows is an error:

u(5, sites)
#> Error:
#> ! u(): `sites` is not a unit the units database knows. A project's own unit is registered when the dictionary that names it is read (rule 4.4.7), or with units::install_unit(). The units package says: In 'sites', 'sites' is not recognized by udunits.

There are two ways to add one. A dictionary entry with that unit registers it when the dictionary is read. The units: table in _weft.yml registers it when the configuration is read, and gives it a name, a plural, a symbol, or a definition. The document above used this _weft.yml:

units:
  sites:
    name: site
    symbol: false
  PSU:
    name: practical salinity unit

symbol: false makes sites print by its name in every form (“12 sites”). The PSU row gives a name to a unit the default table already has, so .uname can print it. Each row takes up to six fields:

Field Sets
name the singular name
plural the plural, when the English rule gets it wrong
symbol the symbol text, or false for none
space whether a space goes between the number and the symbol
is what the unit is: base, a number, or an amount of another unit (4.54609 L)
before true to write the unit before the number

Some unit symbols mean something unexpected to the units package. weft refuses those rather than print a wrong value:

u(5, mt)
#> Error:
#> ! u(): `mt` is read by the units package as a millitonne (`m` + `t`), which is 1 kg. Write `t` for a tonne, or `Mt` for a megatonne. To take that reading, set `unit_defaults: si` in _weft.yml (rule 4.4.20).

weft keeps the units tables in R’s user cache folder (tools::R_user_dir("weft", "cache")) so that a new session starts faster. options(weft.units_cache = FALSE) turns that off.

The dictionary

The dictionary holds the values a project chose, as opposed to values it computed. Each entry has a key, a value, a type and a definition. It lives in dict.yml at the project root. This one has an entry of every type:

writeLines(c(
  "trigger:",
  "  value: 10",
  "  type: quantity",
  "  unit: NTU",
  "  term: turbidity trigger",
  "  definition: \"Turbidity above which a site is reported.\"",
  "reach_len:",
  "  value: 2000",
  "  type: quantity",
  "  unit: m",
  "  display: km",
  "  definition: \"Length of the surveyed reach.\"",
  "min_samples:",
  "  value: 5",
  "  type: number",
  "  definition: \"Fewest samples a site needs in a season.\"",
  "first_year:",
  "  value: 2014",
  "  type: year",
  "  definition: \"First year of the logger record.\"",
  "survey_start:",
  "  value: 2024-09-02",
  "  type: date",
  "  definition: \"First day of the spring survey.\"",
  "catchment:",
  "  value: \"Eastern catchment\"",
  "  type: string",
  "  definition: \"Name used for the study area.\"",
  "  avoid: [\"east catchment\"]",
  "tier_lab:",
  "  value: {ref: Reference, mod: Moderately disturbed, high: Highly disturbed}",
  "  type: labels",
  "  definition: \"Display names for the disturbance tiers.\"",
  "trend_word:",
  "  value:",
  "    - {below: 0.95, phrase: \"a fall in\"}",
  "    - {at_most: 1.05, phrase: \"no change in\"}",
  "    - {phrase: \"a rise in\"}",
  "  type: breaks",
  "  definition: \"Wording for this year's mean over last year's.\""
), "dict.yml")
type value Read as
number a number a number
quantity a number, with a unit a quantity, in its display unit when it has one
year a four-digit year a year, which never gets a thousands mark
date YYYY-MM-DD a Date
string text a string
labels a map from key to phrase a lookup() function
breaks a list of bands, each with below or at_most and a phrase a brk() function

In a knit, weft reads dict.yml itself and makes the object dict, so the prose and the chunks read dict$trigger. At the console, read_dict() reads it:

dict <- read_dict("dict.yml")
dict
#> <weft_dict> dict.yml: 8 keys
#>   trigger  quantity  10 NTU
#>   reach_len  quantity  2 km
#>   min_samples  number  5
#>   first_year  year  2014
#>   survey_start  date  2024-09-02
#>   catchment  string  Eastern catchment
#>   tier_lab  labels  3 labels
#>   trend_word  breaks  3 bands
#> Units registered: NTU
dict$reach_len
#> 2 [km]
dict$first_year + 1
#> [1] 2015
dict$tier_lab("mod")
#> [1] "Moderately disturbed"
dict$trend_word(1.02)
#> [1] "no change in"
fmt_range(range(c(dict$first_year, dict$first_year + 10)))
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "2014–2024"

dict$key matches the key exactly. A key that is not there is an error, never NULL, and the dictionary cannot be changed from R:

dict$triger
#> Error:
#> ! `dict$triger`: no such key in dict.yml (rule 4.1.2). Did you mean `trigger`?
dict$trigger <- 5
#> Error:
#> ! weft: the dictionary is read-only; change dict.yml (rule 4.1.4).

read_dict() checks every entry and reports every problem in the file at once, each with its line:

writeLines(c(
  "depth:", "  value: 010", "  type: number", "  definition: Mean depth.",
  "spot:", "  value: 3", "  type: count", "  definition: A spot check."
), "bad.yml")
read_dict("bad.yml")
#> Error:
#> ! weft: bad.yml: 2 problem(s) in the dictionary
#> bad.yml:1: `depth`: `value` is a whole number written with a leading zero, or in hex or octal; write it in decimal (rule 4.2.1)
#> bad.yml:5: `spot`: `type` `count` is not one of number, quantity, year, date, string, labels, breaks (rule 4.2.1)

Besides the three required fields, an entry may have unit and display (quantities only), decision, term and avoid. decision points at the record of why the value was chosen, such as a GitHub issue number; verify() checks that each pointer resolves. The setting decisions in _weft.yml says where pointers resolve: github (the default), github:<owner>/<repo>, a file pattern such as decisions/{id}-*.md, or a function.

A chapter’s own values

A value that holds for one document only goes in that document’s front matter, under weft: and dict_local:, with a why that says why it is not in the project dictionary. The document above has one. It is read as dict_local$key, never dict$key, so a reader of the source sees at once that the value is local.

The glossary

dict_glossary() writes the dictionary as a Pandoc definition list. A chunk that calls it is the glossary; it needs no results: asis:

cat(dict_glossary(dict))
#> 
#> `catchment` (Eastern catchment)
#> :   Name used for the study area.
#> 
#> `first_year` (2014)
#> :   First year of the logger record.
#> 
#> `min_samples` (5)
#> :   Fewest samples a site needs in a season.
#> 
#> `reach_len` (2 km)
#> :   Length of the surveyed reach.
#> 
#> `survey_start` (2 September 2024)
#> :   First day of the spring survey.
#> 
#> `tier_lab`
#> :   Display names for the disturbance tiers.
#> 
#> `trend_word`
#> :   Wording for this year's mean over last year's.
#> 
#> turbidity trigger (10 NTU)
#> :   Turbidity above which a site is reported.

In a knit, dict_glossary() with no argument uses the knit’s dictionary.

Spellings to avoid

avoid lists spellings that should be the entry’s term, or for a string entry its value. dict_vale() writes them as a rule for the prose linter Vale. It says what it will write first:

dict_vale(dict)
#> weft will write /tmp/RtmpO0nfBb/units-article/styles/Weft/Terms.yml: a Vale substitution rule with 1 avoided spelling(s) from dict.yml.
#> Wrote: /tmp/RtmpO0nfBb/units-article/styles/Weft/Terms.yml
#> Vale uses this rule when .vale.ini, at /tmp/RtmpO0nfBb/units-article, sets StylesPath = styles and lists Weft in BasedOnStyles.
cat(readLines("styles/Weft/Terms.yml"), sep = "\n")
#> # Generated by weft::dict_vale() from dict.yml. Do not edit: change the
#> # `avoid:` fields in dict.yml and run weft::dict_vale() again.
#> extends: substitution
#> message: "Use '%s' instead of '%s' (the project dictionary's spelling)."
#> level: warning
#> ignorecase: false
#> swap:
#>   'east catchment': 'Eastern catchment'

Finding values to put in the dictionary

dict_seed() reads a project’s documents, runs nothing, and lists names that two or more documents assign a literal value to, as candidates for the dictionary:

writeLines(c("```{r}", "trigger <- 10", "n_sites <- 3", "```"), "spring.Rmd")
writeLines(c("```{r}", "trigger <- 10", "n_sites <- 4", "```"), "autumn.Rmd")
dict_seed(c("spring.Rmd", "autumn.Rmd"))[, c("name", "value", "differs", "n")]
#>      name value differs n
#> 1 n_sites  <NA>    TRUE 2
#> 2 trigger    10   FALSE 2

trigger holds one value in both documents, so it is a stipulation that belongs in dict.yml. n_sites differs, and the author decides what it is.

use_dictionary() writes a starter dict.yml and a schema that editors use to check it as you type. See vignette("setup", package = "weft").
